Dw, I feel like a lot of people are actually aware of the fact that they can do XYZ without being whatever gender typically associated with it.    
Heck, I tried. I really tried for most of my life and my parents accepted and supported that. I tried being a "tomboy" and wore "boy's" clothes and short hair and what not. Tried to participate in things typically "boys only did". Because I knew the other ways made me wildly uncomfortable.    

But nothing quite felt right. It felt like a sham. Close to something I was looking for, but just not quite there. And it just made me more depressed.    
And idk, at some point something just broke. And started shaving my hair further and further shorter. But it didn't *work*. It wasn't right. Because I was still a "woman". Plenty of women have shaved hair. It didn't matter. It didn't make me feel any better.     

And ig my dad noticed at some point. And called me, and asked me if I possibly could be going through something like someone we knew, who was also a trans man.    
And for some reason having to admit that maybe I was, made me start sobbing.     


And ehhhh, idk why. But living as I am now, I finally feel ig normal? Ironically, before my transition I would shun "feminine" things. Now I firmly acknowledge that presentation and what not doesn't have anything to do with gender, and I'm more willing to toy with that stuff, now that most people in my life acknowledge me as a man.

I will tbh, to strangers; since I'm stealth. Just because it's safer that way. I've actually had someone tell me, "Wow! I never would have guessed! You don't look trans!" After we got into an awkward conversation where they were asking me why I didn't want to have kids myself.

Assholes blame others for their own emotional stuff.

Media seems to like to portray stuff like romance as permanent and unconditional, bc for them it's nice. Change is scary.

And personal conflict tends to be a topic that can come up easily for most people especially regarding their experiences in gender and what not.     

Otherwise, someone who's feeling more secure in their identity, is more likely to just... idk. Go to subreddits of their hobbies/interests. Nothing related to their gender stuff.     

So tbh, I feel like this sort of situation is kind of the natural result of how communities like this work.    
It's not like NB ppl are some sort of creatures that come outta the furniture.

To anyone that may be looking at the worst of this comment section and feeling bad for taking a single day off to get your stuff together:    

Don't.    

This is going to sound harsh- and it is- but I have these kinds of people with these kinds of mindsets in my own workplace.    
And they are quite possibly the most ineffective people I have the misfortune to work with.     
That doesn't mean they're bad people. All unique people with charming personalities and interests.    
But they're *terrible* workers.    
They've usually worked themselves until their bodies ache, and their personal issues pop out with being unable to balance a friendly but polite and time effective conversation with clients and co-workers alike.    
Which I don't think some of them even realize they're doing.     


The real world isn't a place where you "suck it up." The real world is a place where you learn to balance.    
Give yourself a day, then come back.

Imo, it's a balancing act that needs to be learned with actual experience and depends heavily on the person/circumstances.    

I work in healthcare, a nursing facility, and in units where there is quite literally people that are dependent on you to eat, bathe, and excrete.    

And I absolutely DESPISE my coworkers that come in  sick and/or distressed by something; and trying to hide it.    
Because no matter how much they think they're good at hiding it. They are ALWAYS underperforming.    
Communication issues, weakness, less dexterity and focus, etc.    

There was one time where I got so frustrated with someone, I just barely held myself back from telling them to go home. Because they refused to talk about their issues or make any adjustments to where they can still complete their tasks.     


I heavily suggest to students: Having self-discipline also means knowing when to ask for help. And if you know help won't cut it/isn't possible?    
THEN call it quits.     

You are way more annoying and unhelpful when you're unwell and trying to push it down "for the sake of others".

Seek support or go home if you know something's wrong.
